claims.text: Sliding induces severe plastic deformation and high strain rates in the HEA surface.
Sliding-induced deformation dynamically creates a nanocrystalline or amorphous surface layer.
The refined surface layer has a high density of grain boundaries that provide rapid diffusion pathways for passive-film-forming species.
The refined surface layer rapidly re-establishes a protective passive film.
Mechanical wear removes or disrupts the passive film.
Competition between mechanical film removal and dynamic film reformation governs overall tribo-corrosion degradation.
A Cantor-type CoCrFeMnNi alloy can possess a chromium-derived passive layer.
The proposed coarse-grained, cold-rolled Cantor alloy initially has a stable passive film in a non-aggressive environment.
Chemically formed surface oxide films can materially affect deformation and wear resistance in HEAs.
OCP and EIS measurements before, during, and after sliding can monitor passive-film dynamics.
Combined tribo-corrosion will produce less total degradation than the sum of isolated inert-environment wear and static corrosion.
Dynamic repassivation will reduce the corrosion component of degradation during sliding.
Dynamic repassivation will reduce the wear-rate component relative to the independent-effects baseline.
The mechanism should operate at moderate sliding speeds and corrosivity when repassivation can keep pace with film removal.
The mechanism may fail at extremely high wear rates or in environments aggressive enough to overwhelm passivation kinetics.
Cantor-alloy corrosion resistance can vary with processing-induced microstructure and residual stress.
Passivation and corrosion behavior can depend on alloy composition, particularly chromium content.
Comparing corrosive sliding with inert-environment sliding isolates the effect of simultaneous mechanical wear on passive-film stability.
Absence of the refined surface layer together with total degradation equal to or greater than the additive isolated losses would falsify the proposed mechanism.
